o: A client sending forged session cookies to the origin server
Making the server send HTTP requests to attacker-chosen URLs
Forging TLS certificates in order to intercept server traffic
Injecting SQL through a server-side JSON API request body
questions.x: SSRF abuses a server feature that fetches a URL. The attacker picks the target, so the request comes from the server's own network and can hit internals that the attacker cannot open directly.
questions.h: The S is server-side. The R is request. Who is sending the forged request, and to whose chosen host?

questions.q: Which destination is a typical SSRF target?
o: A public search engine on the open internet
localhost, RFC1918 ranges, or 169.254.x.x metadata
A third-party CDN used only for static assets
The site's own public marketing domain over HTTPS
questions.x: Useful SSRF targets are things the public internet cannot reach: the host itself, 192.168/10.x internals, AWS-style metadata at 169.254.x.x, and internal APIs or admin panels.
questions.h: SSRF is valuable because the server can reach places you cannot. Which of these is not on the public internet?

questions.q: Consider these claims about how SSRF works. (1) The app takes a URL from a parameter. (2) The server then requests that URL. (3) An attacker can swap in an internal address. Which option is correct?
o: All of these statements are true
Only the first claim is true
Only the first two claims are true
Only the third claim is true
questions.x: A typical flow is ?url=https://example.com, the server fetches it, then an attacker changes that value to something like http://localhost/admin. Blind SSRF hides the body. Non-blind SSRF returns it.
questions.h: Which step in that three-part flow is actually optional for SSRF to exist?

questions.q: What is the difference between blind SSRF and non-blind SSRF?
o: Blind SSRF only hits localhost. Non-blind hits other hosts.
Blind SSRF hides the fetch result. Non-blind returns it.
Blind SSRF uses POST requests only. Non-blind uses GET only.
Blind SSRF needs a valid login. Non-blind works without one.
questions.x: Non-blind SSRF shows the attacker the body the server fetched. Blind SSRF still makes the server send the request, but you infer success with DNS callbacks, timing, or errors instead of reading the response.
questions.h: Blind means you cannot see the fetched body. Did the server still make the request?

questions.q: Why is 169.254.x.x a common SSRF goal in the cloud?
o: It is a public DNS resolver that logs every outbound query
It can reach instance metadata that is not on the internet
It is the default VPC gateway used to leave the private net
It is an anycast address that maps only to the app's CDN
questions.x: Cloud metadata lives on a link-local address reachable from the instance, not from the public internet. An SSRF to that address can return credentials and other instance data.
questions.h: Which special address is only useful from inside a cloud VM and is known for returning instance credentials?
